intro: Martial arts carry names, and names can be claimed. A Kodokan certificate, a Kukkiwon registry number, a U.S. trademark and a UNESCO heritage listing each say that someone holds a name. Sometimes those records agree. Sometimes, as with the several groups that have called themselves the International Taekwon-Do Federation since 2002, they point in different directions.

Martial arts also carry memory. Karate grew in the Ryukyu Kingdom before Japan annexed it in 1879. Brazil's 1890 penal code made capoeira a crime two years after slavery ended. Japanese American judo clubs met inside incarceration camps after 1942. Women and Black athletes waited decades for the titles and ranks their skill had earned.

In this unit you will weigh dated records against legends and feelings. You will read laws, court cases, rank registers and heritage lists as evidence. By the end, you will be able to argue who holds a martial art's name, and how a school can honor its founders while telling hard history factually.
bigQuestion: Who has the right to claim a martial art's name and its past, and what evidence should decide?

timeline.t: Satsuma forces invade the Ryukyu Kingdom
Japan annexes the Ryukyu Kingdom as Okinawa Prefecture
Kanō Jigorō opens the Kodokan at Eishō-ji in Tokyo
Brazil's penal code makes capoeira a crime
Jack Johnson wins the world heavyweight boxing title in Sydney
Okinawan teachers in Naha agree to write karate as empty hand
Executive Order 9066 leads to the incarceration of Japanese Americans
Allied occupation officials dissolve the Dai Nippon Butokukai
Choi Hong-hi founds the International Taekwon-Do Federation in Seoul
The Amateur Sports Act gives the USOC control of the word Olympic
Women win Olympic judo medals for the first time, in Barcelona
UNESCO lists the capoeira circle as intangible cultural heritage

words.d: a line of teachers and students through which a school's name passes
"license of complete transmission"; the top written license in many old Japanese schools
a numbered rank counted upward from first dan
an official list that records who holds which rank or right
a word, name or symbol that shows who offers a product or service
the common name for a whole kind of thing, which no one can own as a trademark
an organization that joins many schools or national groups under shared rules
living practices, such as festivals, songs and crafts, that a community passes on
a community living far from its homeland that keeps ties to it
when one country takes over another territory and makes it part of itself
when a foreign power governs a country after a war; in Japan, 1945 to 1952
a barrier that kept Black athletes out of contests or titles

test.q: What did the Kodokan introduce in 1883?
test.why: Kanō gave the first dan grades in 1883 to Saigō Shirō and Tomita Tsunejirō.

test.q: Which body issues taekwondo poom certificates?
test.why: The Kukkiwon in Seoul issues dan and poom certificates.

test.q: Which word could a school register as a trademark?
choices: a special school name with its own logo
test.why: A school's own name can be a trademark; generic art names cannot.

test.q: Which 1987 Supreme Court case concerned the word Olympic?
choices: San Francisco Arts and Athletics v. USOC
test.why: The Court ruled for the U.S. Olympic Committee in San Francisco Arts and Athletics v. USOC.
World Taekwondo, founded in 1973, governs Olympic taekwondo.

test.q: What did South Korea's National Assembly name taekwondo in 2018?
test.why: A 2018 law named taekwondo South Korea's national sport.

test.q: What does IOC recognition of IFMA in 2021 mean?
choices: Muay Thai is on every Olympic program.
The IOC accepts IFMA as Muay Thai's world governing body.
IFMA became part of the Kukkiwon.
test.why: Recognition accepts IFMA as the governing body without adding the sport to the Games.

test.q: Why is the 1936 Naha meeting good evidence?
choices: It has a date, a place, named people and a printed report.
test.why: The meeting has a date, place, named teachers and a newspaper report.

test.q: What happened to the Ryukyu Kingdom in 1879?
test.why: Japan ended the kingdom in 1879 and made it Okinawa Prefecture.

test.q: What did Brazil's 1890 penal code do?
choices: It made capoeira the national sport.
It made practicing capoeira in public a crime.
test.why: The 1890 code punished capoeira practiced in streets and squares.

test.q: When were martial arts returned to Japanese schools, starting with judo?
test.why: Judo returned to Japanese school programs in 1950, during the occupation.

test.q: What did the Civil Liberties Act of 1988 do?
choices: It ended the occupation of Japan.
It apologized and paid survivors of the camps.
test.why: The 1988 law apologized and paid 20,000 dollars to each surviving person held.

test.q: In which year did women first win Olympic judo medals?
test.why: Women won Olympic judo medals for the first time at the 1992 Barcelona Games.

test.q: Which boxer broke the heavyweight color line in 1908?
test.why: Jack Johnson beat Tommy Burns in Sydney in 1908.

test.q: Why do taekwondo schools remember Choi Hong-hi differently?
choices: His life crossed a divided Korea.
test.why: Choi's ties to both South and North Korea shape how different groups remember him.

write.prompt: Pick one martial art from this unit. Who has the strongest claim to its name, and how should a school tell its hard history? Cite at least two dated records, such as the 1936 Naha meeting, the 1890 Brazilian penal code, the 2002 ITF split or the 1987 Supreme Court case.
tips: Name each record you cite and give its date.
Say what question each record can answer and what it cannot.
Attribute every view to the group or person who holds it.
Label legends as legends and set them beside the records.
Use unit words such as lineage, registry, trademark and annexation.
